scenario: A 76-year-old man has exertional syncope. He has a harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border that radiates to the neck, and his carotid upstroke is slow. A classmate calls it mitral regurgitation because both are systolic.
question: Which valve lesion fits the radiation, and why does the carotid upstroke matter?
options: Outflow obstruction, with a delayed carotid peak
Mitral regurgitation, which radiates to the neck and slows the carotid
Aortic regurgitation, so the murmur should be diastolic
Hypertrophic obstruction that gets louder when he squats
A flow murmur of anemia, so the upstroke should be bounding
correctAnswer: Outflow obstruction, with a delayed carotid peak
citation: Hall JE, Hall ME. Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology. 14th ed. Elsevier; 2021.
examTakeaway: Severe aortic stenosis is a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the base that radiates to the carotids, with a slow carotid upstroke.
